The report combines a live title-based annual query, monthly news queries, news-country resolution, a bounded evidence packet, a subject-level orientation tally and a scenario projection. It does not claim a systematic review. It does not infer missing evidence from an empty search result, or infer zeros for countries or periods omitted by a tool. The aim is to provide an auditable draft whose conclusions remain inside the bounds of retrieved material.

Data and methods

The research-attention source was Prism’s historical_analysis feature, which queried Prism research index records for 2017–2025. Its subject phrases were “sugar-sweetened beverages” and “sugary drinks”; its outcome phrases were “obesity” and “type 2 diabetes.” The matching rule was title matching, requiring any phrase from each list, case-insensitively. The returned annual record count is not a deduplicated study count and was not normalized by total yearly corpus volume. The query output warned that changing corpus size and enrichment coverage were not controlled and that year bounds are safe query defaults rather than a guarantee of complete coverage. [c1]

The news-attention source was Prism’s news_trends feature. An initial query using the whole phrase “sugar-sweetened beverages obesity type 2 diabetes” returned no data, so it was not treated as a measured series. A query for “sugary drinks” returned monthly article counts from January 2017 through April 2026. The tool’s match mode was “mention.” The tool censored at June 1, 2026, explaining that more recent months would be incomplete because news ingestion and enrichment lag. Monthly values are not equivalent to diabetes-specific coverage, and the publication-count query is not an indicator of public awareness. [c3]

The news-geography source was Prism’s news_geography feature with the term “sugary drinks,” country level, and the same January 2017 to May 2026 exclusive window. Its output defines the label as the place an article is about, resolved by the pipeline, not where it was published. It returned country counts for 1,603 placed articles among 3,927 matched articles. Since less than half of matched articles received a country label, the distribution is partial. Resolved labels may include pipeline errors; the tool itself warns about place-resolution collisions. [c5]

The health-evidence source was Prism’s research_packet feature with the claim “Sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes,” subject phrases “sugar-sweetened beverages” and “sugary drinks,” outcome phrase “type 2 diabetes,” years 2000–2025, limit 10 and read enabled. The packet used title matching and returned a bounded discovery set rather than an exhaustive review. The tool says title matching misses synonyms and studies with uninformative titles, metadata may carry upstream errors, and absence from the sample is not evidence of absence. Its quotes were text-verified, while stance labels were identified as model interpretation. [c2]

A separate Prism find_counter_evidence call used the same central claim and a five-document limit. The returned tally had no verified claim-level support or contradiction and noted that only seven papers covered both poles, while health-factor evidence was unavailable. The wider subject-level corpus was described as 1,090 papers over 2017–2025, with orientation and contribution labels; those values are not treated as a claim-specific evidence balance. [c4]

The scenario source was Prism’s trend_scenarios feature, using the saved history identifier from the annual research query and a three-year horizon. It compared no-change and linear drift by expanding-window one-step-ahead backtests. It selected no-change because that baseline had lower MAE on the four returned folds. The forecast bounds were computed as sensitivity ranges based on the worst one-step error times the horizon; they are not confidence intervals and have no probability interpretation. [c7]

The session attempted a research browse scoped to India, but this tool interprets its geographic scope as a word appearing in a paper title. It is therefore not a first-author affiliation-country query. No successful query retrieved journal-country or patent-assignee-country counts. No tool output provided an article-month-to-annual aligned series for correlation, nor a usable complete monthly export. No independent article publication-date or patent-lag calibration was performed. These absences define the analysis boundary, not evidence that the lanes have no records.

Results

The annual research series contains 14 records in 2017, 1 in 2018, 17 in 2019, 9 in 2020, 5 in 2021, 9 in 2022, 10 in 2023, 18 in 2024 and 16 in 2025. The absolute difference between 2017 and 2025 is 2 records; the relative endpoint change is 14.3%. These calculations describe the queried title matches only. The annual sequence is irregular, and it does not support a simple claim of steadily increasing output. [c1]

The news trend output covers January 2017–April 2026 for “sugary drinks.” The tool reports 1,608 articles in total, with 9 articles in January 2017, 21 in April 2026, a peak of 49 in October 2025, and late-third volume 2.09 times early-third volume. The published peak and endpoint are not measurements of the central diabetes claim because the matching rule is a broader mention query. The query was censored before the incomplete May 2026 month, so no apparent terminal collapse is plotted. [c3]

Because the research series is annual and the news series is monthly, their matching rules differ, and the monthly full vector was not carried into a harmonized analysis, no correlation coefficient, lag estimate or significance test is reported. Endpoint movement in the two sources is directionally positive, but that is a qualitative comparison, not a quantitative relationship. [c1] [c3]

The evidence packet’s meta-analysis excerpt compared individuals in the highest SSB intake quantile—most often one to two servings per day—with those in the lowest quantile—none or less than one serving per month. It reported RR 1.26 with 95% CI 1.12–1.41. A second packet record reported the same number, and a third older item reproduced it; these records are not counted as separate pooled estimates here. The retrieved excerpt does not give the pooled study count or participant total, so neither is supplied. [c2] [r1]

A prospective study of Thai adults reported that women consuming SSBs once daily or more, compared with rarely, had higher type 2 diabetes incidence at eight-year follow-up (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.5–3.9); the excerpt explicitly says the relationship was not observed in men. The result qualifies the claim by sex and population, but its excerpt does not establish the reason for the difference. [c2] [r2] A cross-sectional risk-score study among tertiary students in Abeokuta reported large odds ratios for several drinks, including fruit drinks OR 15.2 with a very wide interval. Since the stated outcome was FINDRISC-derived risk rather than observed incident diabetes, this estimate is not interpreted as an incidence effect. [c2] [r3]

Within the ten-document evidence packet, the returned stance classification is nine supporting and one qualifying, with no contradicting source. Because the packet was bounded and the source-fit/stance process was not independent fact-checking, that tally is descriptive of this packet only. The distinct counter-evidence call returned no verified claim-level supporting, contradicting or qualifying entries and one unread record; it specifically cautioned that only seven papers addressed both poles. The apparent difference between these tool outputs shows why neither should be turned into a comprehensive vote count. [c2] [c4]

The subject-level orientation summary covers 1,090 papers in the typed research corpus from 2017–2025. It reports 202 supporting, 317 qualifying, 23 contradicting and 548 neutral labels. These are not claim-level counts: the tool states its lane is the subject, including SSB papers that do not establish the SSB-to-diabetes relation. The health-evidence extraction was unavailable, so the requested direction-of-risk-factor claim tally cannot be reported. [c4]

For news geography, 1,603 of 3,927 matching articles received a country-about assignment. The top listed country counts were United States 1,026, United Kingdom 343, Mexico 144, Australia 134, India 129, France 107, New Zealand 78 and South Africa 68. Since this is an article-about lane and not a publication or author lane, it does not reveal where researchers or publishers are located. [c5]

The no-change forecast starts from the 2025 observed value of 16 matching research records. Its central path is 16 in each forecast year, 2026–2028. Sensitivity ranges are 8–24 for 2026, 0–32 for 2027 and 0–40 for 2028. In the backtest, no-change MAE was 3.75, compared with linear-drift MAE 4.872, across four expanding-window folds from 2022 through 2025. Because the forecast is conditional on the title-matched count series and the error ranges are sensitivity calculations, it is not a forecast of diabetes risk or SSB consumption. [c7]

Discussion

The most defensible interpretation is that the retrieved epidemiological literature supports an association between greater SSB intake and type 2 diabetes risk, with a pooled estimate above the null and a prospective cohort result that varies by sex. The meta-analysis and cohort answer different questions: the former aggregates evidence across included populations and intake contrasts, while the latter supplies population-specific prospective evidence. Their agreement on direction is meaningful, but the available excerpts do not permit a full appraisal of confounding control, exposure measurement or study overlap. [r1] [r2]

Other published syntheses have also examined SSB intake and metabolic outcomes. The packet’s retrieved meta-analysis is the quantitative anchor here; the 2025 global-burden article states that SSB consumption is associated with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, but the excerpt does not provide a causal design or a number suitable for comparing with the pooled RR. The report therefore uses that article as context rather than as an independent causal estimate. [r4]

The attention findings should not be read as evidence of a public-health trend. Research publication counts are title-query outputs, and the news query measures mention volume. Both move upward between selected endpoints, but neither measures exposure prevalence, diabetes incidence, policy adoption or the intensity of public concern. The latest news period was deliberately censored at April 2026 because ingestion and country enrichment lag publication. The annual research count extends through 2025, leaving nearly two years between its latest full observation and the report date. [c1] [c3] [c5]

The geography measurement is more limited still. The news country-about lane describes the countries news items discuss. A country may be discussed by a foreign publisher, and a paper about India may have authors affiliated elsewhere. Since no first-author, journal-country or assignee-country counts were successfully queried, the requested mismatch between where research is conducted and where it is reported cannot be measured. The map therefore displays one lane alone and preserves the distinction required for interpretation. [c5] [c6]

For the next research phase, the highest-value investments are likely to be those that reduce uncertainty in causal interpretation and improve evidence transportability: prospective designs with repeated dietary measurement; transparent treatment of substitution and energy balance; sufficiently powered subgroup analysis; and policy evaluations connecting price or access changes to actual intake and diabetes outcomes. These priorities follow from the observed limits in study-specific excerpts and missing risk-factor extraction. They are recommendations, not outcomes measured by the corpus. [c2] [c4]

Limitations

Data end dates differ by source. The annual title-match research data end in 2025, roughly 1.8 years before 2026-10-23. The monthly “sugary drinks” news data end in April 2026; the query window excludes May 2026 and later due to ingest censoring. The article-about enrichment boundary is May 2026, but a month’s calendar completion alone does not establish complete news ingestion. A later rerun after source-specific completeness checks could alter the endpoint comparisons. [c1] [c3] [c5]

Research coverage is title-based and bounded. It can miss studies whose title uses different terminology, studies that discuss an outcome only in the abstract or full text, and duplicate bibliographic records. The discovery packet is not a systematic review; it does not provide a complete eligibility flow, duplicate resolution, risk-of-bias assessment, or independent extraction. A registered search across bibliographic and clinical databases, followed by deduplication and full-text screening, could change the evidence balance and the selected effect estimate. [c1] [c2]

The news source’s coverage and matching are also incomplete. “Sugary drinks” is a broad term and may match stories that do not discuss diabetes, while omitting coverage using other wording. Only 40.8% of matched articles had resolved country labels. Place recognition can make errors, and incomplete enrichment can make a country appear underrepresented. A validated sample of article text and publisher metadata, plus alternate phrase queries, would improve these measurements. [c3] [c5]

The geography lanes are incomplete by design of the obtained data. Article-about country is measured; first-author affiliation country, journal country and patent assignee country are not. Therefore there is no study-versus-reporting mismatch estimate and no evidence-based four-lane ranking. The India-filtered browse used title text and cannot be treated as author-country evidence. A consistent record-level extraction with verified ISO country mappings for all four lanes would close this gap. [c5] [c6]

No patent publication-lag analysis was performed, and no patent series was retrieved. Patent counts can be affected by filing and publication delays, jurisdictional choices and assignee normalization; without a query and a lag-aware window, a patent trajectory cannot be interpreted. Patent data should be collected with a conservative end date and assignee-country validation before any comparison with research or news is attempted.

The forecast has a short history, four one-step backtest folds and no independent holdout. Its baseline selection and error summaries use the same observed series. The sensitivity ranges are not confidence intervals; they do not include structural breaks, seasonality, changing indexing practices or future corpus changes. More history, a predeclared evaluation window and multiple rolling-origin backtests could change the selected method or widen uncertainty. [c7]

Finally, evidence is thin for a source-independent claim-level tally in the material retrieved here. The absent extracted risk-factor claim results do not show that no such evidence exists. Full-text systematic screening, a formal risk-of-bias assessment and independent evidence extraction could either strengthen the causal conclusion or identify material counterevidence. [c2] [c4]

C. Research article

Abstract

Background: Sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) are widely held to raise the risk of type 2 diabetes, yet the volume, geography and tier of the evidence have rarely been measured together with news attention and patents. Methods: I ran title-matched queries on a research-and-news intelligence server. Research counts came from Prism research index titles for 2017–2025 [c2][c9]. News counts came from monthly mention series for January 2023–May 2026 [c3]. Evidence was ranked by study tier with verbatim quotes [c4][c5]. Geography used the health literature index first-author and journal-country lanes [c6], news placement [c7] and patent assignee rows [c6][c13]. A three-year projection used a no-change baseline [c8]. Results: Titled SSB-with-diabetes/obesity papers rose from 24 to 38 per year [c2], while 843 news articles appeared over the news window [c3]. Only 3 papers covered both sides of the claim [c4]. The strongest document, a meta-analysis, reported RR 1.25 per serving [r1]. Nothing contradicted the claim among documents read [c5]. First authorship was concentrated in China and the United States [c6], whereas news placed Nigeria, Mexico and South Africa in the top five [c7]. The patent lane was empty [c4]. A flat projection of 38 records per year (range 14–62 by 2028) was selected [c8]. Conclusions: The direction of association is consistent, but direct evidence is thin, and attention and authorship are geographically mismatched. All counts are title-matched records and not effect estimates.

Introduction

Sugar-sweetened beverages are a recurrent target of nutrition policy because they deliver rapidly absorbed sugar with little satiety, and because intake is measurable and modifiable. A causal link from SSB intake to type 2 diabetes has been examined in prospective cohorts and pooled in meta-analyses. A 2025 dose-response meta-analysis reported a risk ratio of 1.25 (95% CI 1.17–1.35) per additional serving at moderate certainty [r1]. A systematic review in Asian populations reported higher risk for the highest versus lowest consumption category, which was attenuated but persisted after BMI adjustment [r2]. An earlier meta-analysis, cited here from memory rather than retrieved in this session, reported the association persisting after adjustment for adiposity [r3].

Evidence synthesis for decision making also asks different questions: how much attention a claim receives, who produces it, who reads about it, and whether commercial activity follows. These questions belong to the science of science. They are seldom answered with the same method, window and tier labels across research, news and patents. This article does so for one claim: that SSB consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes. It poses five research questions covering attention, evidence, geography, trajectory and synthesis. It keeps a strict rule: each number must either trace to a query run for this article or to a cited reference. Where a measure could not be obtained, the article reports a null.

The article makes two contributions. First, it quantifies how thin the directly relevant literature is, with only 3 papers covering both the exposure and the outcome in the typed corpus [c4], while many more concern SSBs alone (283 typed papers) [c4]. Second, it shows the geographic mismatch between where the subject is studied and where it is reported [c6][c7]. It does not estimate the causal effect of SSBs, and it does not perform a new meta-analysis.

Data and methods

Overview. All data came from one research-and-news intelligence server, queried on 2026-10-23. Thirteen calls were made (c1–c13, declared in the manifest). No analysis beyond these was performed. The patent lane was queried, and returned nothing. No full-text reading, manual screening or independent statistical modelling was carried out.

Freshness (c1). A freshness check reported the news ingest tail relative to a monthly baseline of 2,649,886 articles. June 2026 held 19.4% of baseline, July 2.0% and August 0.4% [c1]. The default report cutoff was 2026-06-01 [c1].

Research counts (c2, c9). Yearly counts of Prism research index records for 2017–2025, matching titles case-insensitively. Subject phrases: "sugar-sweetened beverages", "sugar-sweetened beverage", "sugary drinks". c2 additionally required an outcome phrase in the title ("type 2 diabetes", "diabetes", "obesity"); c9 applied the subject phrases only. Records are not de-duplicated studies [c2][c9]. Note that "type 2 diabetes" is a subset of "diabetes", so the outcome filter is effectively diabetes or obesity.

News series (c3). Monthly article counts, critical-tone counts, and positive and negative polarity counts for the term "sugar-sweetened beverages" with mention matching, January 2023 to May 2026 (end exclusive 2026-06-01). The tool excludes partial boundary buckets from growth calculations [c3]. For plotting, I omit May 2026 as the newest month.

Evidence (c4, c5, c11, c12). The claim "sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes" was run through the evidence retrieval tool, with read=True. This applies four retrieval lanes, tiers each document by study design, and labels it supports, contradicts, qualifies or unrelated against the claim. Each label is accompanied by a sentence quoted verbatim and verified against the abstract [c4]. The tool reports tallies and a tier-weighted tally [c4][c5]. A counter-evidence call returned the corpus orientation mix and any contradicting documents [c5]. A statistics call extracted verbatim figures [c11]. A citation call produced reference metadata [c12]. Quote verification confirms the quotation, not the interpretation [c4].

Stance (c10). Orientation shares across 536 stance-typed papers matched to four phrases ("sugar-sweetened beverages", "sugar-sweetened drinks", "sugar-sweetened soft drinks", "sugar-sweetened beverage consumption") for 2017–2025 [c10]. The typed corpus begins in 2017.

Geography (c6, c7, c13). The "studied" lane is the country of the first author's affiliation in the health literature index. The "published" lane is the journal country. The "reported" lane is the country an article is about, from news placement for May 2024–May 2026. The "patented" lane is assignee country. These lanes are never summed [c6][c7][c13]. The research lane was queried for the central claim (c6) and for the broader term "sugar-sweetened beverages" (c13). Tables return only the top 12 rows. The news placement query returned the top 25 [c7].

Projection (c8). A scenario tool took the saved series c2 and ran expanding-window one-step backtests of two baselines (no-change; linear drift), choosing the lower mean absolute error. Sensitivity bands use the worst one-step backtest error times the horizon [c8]. They are not probabilities.

Derived quantities. Shares of top-12 research papers, percentage changes, calendar-year news totals, the 3-point Pearson correlation and day gaps were calculated by me from the returned values. They carry the tags of their inputs.

What I did not do. I did not run a patent search beyond the title-match count and assignee table returned by the tools. I did not use disease-factor direction counts, as none matched [c5]. I did not retrieve the full text of any paper.

Results

Attention. Titled SSB-with-diabetes/obesity records numbered 24 (2017), 9 (2018), 27 (2019), 26 (2020), 13 (2021), 17 (2022), 23 (2023), 31 (2024) and 38 (2025) [c2]. This is +58.3% from 2017 to 2025 (derived) [c2]. SSB-titled records overall were 204, 167, 279, 328, 265, 297, 287, 243 and 311 across the same years [c9]. News counted 843 articles from January 2023 to May 2026, of which 625 were critical [c3]. The peak was 49 in October 2025, and the minimum was 4 in June 2024 [c3]. The ratio of late-third to early-third volume was 1.23 [c3]. The 2023–2025 correlation between the research and news series was 0.67 on 3 points (derived) [c2][c3], which carries no inferential weight.

Evidence. The strongest document read was a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts, which reported: "Each additional serving of SSB and fruit juice was associated with a higher risk of T2D (risk ratio [RR]: 1.25; 95% CI: 1.17, 1.35 and RR: 1.05; 95% CI: >1.00, 1.11, respectively; moderate certainty)." [r1] It also reported inverse associations for total sugar (RR 0.96; 0.94–0.98; low certainty) and sucrose (RR 0.95; 0.91–<1.00; moderate certainty) per 20 g/d [c11][r1]. The Asia review reported RR 1.51 (1.15–1.98; I² 76%) before and 1.38 (1.09–1.73; I² 56%) after BMI adjustment [r2]. Of 16 documents retrieved, 2 supported the claim, 0 contradicted and 0 qualified it. Twelve were unrelated, which reflects the retrieval of SSB-only papers [c5]. The tier-weighted tally was 10 for and 0 against [c5]. Among 283 typed SSB papers the labels were 55 supporting, 73 qualifying, 5 contradicting and 150 neutral, a 27.6% contested share [c4]. Orientation shares among 536 papers were descriptive 44.8%, problem-identifying 17.7%, promising 17.5%, cautionary 10.6%, comparative 4.3%, critical 3.0% and breakthrough 2.1% (derived) [c10]. The disease-factor direction tally was unavailable [c5].

Geography. First-author country counts (top 12) led with China 1,980, United States 1,960, United Kingdom 520, Japan 439, India 421 and Germany 418 [c6]. Journal-country counts led with England 3,716, United States 3,325, Switzerland 1,326 and Netherlands 1,011 [c6]. News placement for the term was led by the United States (141), Nigeria (69), the United Kingdom (40), Mexico (30), South Africa (28), India (17) and China (16) [c7]. The patent assignee table was empty [c6][c13]. The tool lists 0 title-matched patents for 2005–2024 [c4]. The research-share against news-share contrast was 26.5% against 2.8% for China (derived) and 5.6% against 2.9% for India (derived) [c6][c7].

Trajectory. The no-change baseline had backtest MAE 6.25 against 7.08 for drift over folds for 2022–2025 [c8]. Central values were 38 for each of 2026, 2027 and 2028, with sensitivity ranges 30–46, 22–54 and 14–62 [c8].

Source mix. The claim lane held 11,867 the health literature index records (1990–2025), 283 typed research papers (2017–2025), 297 readable papers with abstracts, 127 news articles (2019–2026-06), and 0 patents and 0 preprints [c4].

Discussion

The retrieved top-tier evidence agrees in direction with the central claim. A dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts reported RR 1.25 per serving [r1], and an Asian systematic review reported elevated risk that persisted after BMI adjustment [r2]. This is consistent with an earlier meta-analysis from memory that reported an association persisting after adjusting for adiposity [r3], although I did not retrieve that source and do not repeat its numbers. These sources are observational syntheses, so the association is not proof of causation. The meta-analysis grades its own certainty as moderate [r1].

The finding that total sugar and sucrose are inversely associated with type 2 diabetes, while SSBs are positive [r1][c11], shows why a claim phrased at the level of "sugar" is weaker than one phrased at the level of "beverages". This matters for reviewers: contested-share figures in the typed corpus (27.6%) [c4] do not mean the SSB association is disputed. They partly reflect papers that qualify or contextualise the claim, such as total-sugar findings.

The scarcity of papers covering both sides of the claim (3) [c4] is partly a title-matching artefact. Many diabetes-outcome studies say "sweetened beverages" or "soft drinks" in other forms, or sit inside broader dietary titles. The retrieval tool excluded several phrasings after audit found no title match [c4]. The scarcity should therefore be read as a retrieval limit as much as a literature gap.

The geographic mismatch has policy implications. News places Nigeria, Mexico and South Africa in its top five [c7], countries with active beverage-tax or labelling debate (est.), yet none is among the top 12 first-author countries [c6]. Trials of interventions to reduce SSB consumption with India-affiliated authors exist, including a pictorial-warning intervention that reduced reported parental purchases from 55% to 25% [r4] and a school-based meta-analysis in which all intervention types reduced SSB consumption [r5]. Both measure consumption and not diabetes incidence, so they show feasibility, not health benefit.

Attention in the research literature has been steady rather than explosive. Titled records grew by 58.3% over eight years [c2], and the SSB-titled literature as a whole grew by 52.5% [c9]. News is episodic [c3]. A reader cannot infer from the 2023–2025 correlation that either drives the other [c2][c3].

For funders, the data support a shift in emphasis. The association question appears well served by existing syntheses. What the retrieved record lacks is direct, tiered evidence connecting policy to diabetes outcomes, and research originating in the places where the topic is in the news. The patent lane's emptiness [c4] should not be read as an absence of commercial activity. It reflects title matching and publication lag.

Limitations

Data end dates and gap to today. The research series ends in 2025, which is 296 days before today (derived). The news series ends in May 2026, 145 days before today (derived). Ingest volumes fell to 19.4%, 2.0% and 0.4% of baseline for June to August 2026 [c1]. May 2026 (7 articles) [c3] is the newest month and may be incomplete. I did not plot it. Any conclusion about 2026 attention is therefore unsupported.

Title matching. Research counts match phrases in titles only [c2][c9]. They miss studies that use other wording, and the outcome filter in c2 captures all diabetes or obesity titles, not only type 2 diabetes. A count is a record, not a study, not a result, and not a measure of consensus [c2].

Evidence reading. Only 2 documents were read as relevant to the claim [c5]. Quote verification confirms the sentence exists, not that the model's stance label is correct [c4]. Population and period were not stated in the abstract sentences returned (null) [c11]. No direction tally from extracted claims was available [c5]. A new meta-analysis was not run.

Lanes and coverage. The studied and published lanes come from the health literature index first-author and journal country, not from the whole research corpus. The tables list only the top 12 rows [c6], so India's journal-country value is bounded but not known. The news lane places 51.9% of matched articles (270 of 520) [c7], and its place resolution can collide with acronyms [c7]. The research table and news table cover different windows and terms, so cross-lane share comparisons are indicative.

Patents. The patent lane returned no rows [c4][c6][c13]. Patent documents publish roughly 18 months after filing (est.), so recent activity would be absent even if present. A title-based match would also miss claims-level coverage.

Projection. Four backtest folds, used for both selection and error estimation, no independent holdout, and bands that are not confidence intervals [c8]. The series is a count of records and not corpus-normalised.

What would change the conclusions. A high-tier contradicting meta-analysis would lower the confidence in the verdict. A broader phrase list would raise the count of papers covering both sides of the claim. A fuller geography table would change the mismatch figures. A claim-level patent search would change the patent finding. Data after May 2026 would change the news trajectory.
